---
title: "From outcomes to distributions"
---

The [foundations module](../foundations/index.qmd) gave us a probability space $\langle\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P}\rangle$. But a linguistic outcome in $\Omega$ may be a complete token, utterance, or annotated tree, while the next analysis may need only its duration, case, or dependency length. How do we move from the complete outcome to the particular property named in the research question?

A random variable maps each outcome to a value without replacing the outcome that supports it. It is a measurable function from outcomes to values, so questions about those values correspond to events in $\mathcal F$.

For a pronoun-token outcome space, a case variable can be defined by

$$
C(\omega)
\equiv
\text{the annotated case value of token }\omega.
$$

If $\mathcal X_C$ is the set of case values attested under the declared filtering rule, its value space and sigma-algebra are

$$
\mathcal G_C\equiv 2^{\mathcal X_C}.
$$

Now take any set of case values $B\in\mathcal G_C$. The event we can assign probability to is the set of pronoun outcomes that $C$ sends into $B$, that is, the preimage $C^{-1}(B)$. Thus the distribution of $C$ assigns $B$ the probability

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\in B)
\equiv
\mathbb{P}\!\left(C^{-1}(B)\right).
$$

As a function of $B$, this assignment is a probability measure on $\langle\mathcal X_C,\mathcal G_C\rangle$. We retain $\mathbb{P}$ for the probability measure on $\langle\Omega,\mathcal F\rangle$ and introduce no second measure symbol. Expressions such as $\mathbb{P}(C=c)$ abbreviate the corresponding preimage events. Lowercase $p$ and $q$ denote PMFs; lowercase $f$ and $g$ denote PDFs; uppercase $F$ and $G$ denote CDFs. These conventions stay fixed throughout the module.

Keep five roles separate throughout the chapter:

| Role | Typical notation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| random variable | $X$ | a function of a not-yet-observed outcome |
| realized value | $x$ | the value observed for one outcome |
| parameter | $\theta$ | a fixed but possibly unknown feature of a model |
| statistic | $T(\mathbf X)$ | a random function of a random sample |
| estimate | $T(\mathbf x)=\widehat\theta$ | the statistic evaluated on observed data |

The canonical data dossiers are the [CMUdict pronunciation
entries](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes),
[Hillenbrand durations](continuous-random-variables.qmd#hillenbrand-vowel-duration),
[Turkish UniMorph population](hypergeometric-distribution.qmd#a-finite-turkish-morphology-population),
[English dative tokens](poisson-distribution.qmd#the-dative-data), and [Provo
word positions](uniform-distribution.qmd#provo-modeled-predictability).

## Random variables and one-variable distributions

We first explain [why random variables are needed](why-random-variables.qmd) and then give the [measurable-function definition](defining-random-variables.qmd). These pages assume the foundations treatment of [event spaces and sigma-algebras](../foundations/event-spaces.qmd). The next pages introduce [discrete random variables](discrete-random-variables.qmd) and their [probability mass functions](probability-mass-functions.qmd), followed by [absolutely continuous random variables](continuous-random-variables.qmd) and their [probability density functions](probability-density-functions.qmd). A page on [cumulative distribution functions](cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd) then gives the representation shared by both types. This order states what values are possible and immediately specifies how probability is assigned to them.

## Expectations and moments

Once a distribution has been represented, we can ask what features of it one number might summarize. The [expected value](expected-values.qmd) is an integral with respect to a probability distribution when that integral exists. The notes then develop [expectations of functions](expectation-of-functions.qmd), [linearity of expectation](linearity-of-expectation.qmd), and [failure of finite expectations](when-expectations-fail.qmd). [Variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd), [standard deviation](standard-deviation.qmd), and [central moments](central-moments.qmd) summarize specified powers of centered values. Each summary assumes the relevant expectation exists.

## Distribution families

We next reuse those objects in particular observation models. The discrete families are [categorical](bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd), [Bernoulli](bernoulli-distribution.qmd), [binomial](binomial-distribution.qmd), [hypergeometric](hypergeometric-distribution.qmd), [geometric](geometric-distribution.qmd), [negative binomial](negative-binomial-distribution.qmd), and [Poisson](poisson-distribution.qmd). Their supports and probability mass functions differ because they represent different observation processes. The page order moves from one finite-category draw to totals, waits, and exposure-based counts.

The continuous families are [uniform](uniform-distribution.qmd), [beta](beta-distribution.qmd), [normal](normal-distribution.qmd), [chi-squared](chi-squared-distribution.qmd), and [Student's t](student-t-distribution.qmd). Each page states the support, parameterization, and density or defining construction before using the family. The [sampling pages](inverse-transform-sampling.qmd) then show how a CDF turns a basic uniform draw into a draw from another distribution and how a [random seed](random-seeds.qmd) makes the computational realization reproducible.

## Joint distributions

Finally, we move from one variable to several. A [joint distribution](joint-probability.qmd) preserves value pairings from the same outcome. [Marginalization](marginal-distributions.qmd) sums or integrates out one coordinate. [Conditional independence](conditional-independence.qmd) states that one conditional distribution is invariant to an additional conditioning variable. [Conditional expectation](conditional-expectation.qmd), [covariance](covariance.qmd), and [correlation](correlation.qmd) summarize features of conditional or joint distributions. These pages rely on the foundations definitions of [joint event probability](../foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd#the-four-joint-events), [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd#conditioning-as-rescaling), and [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent), so they give only working reminders of those ideas.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) records the prerequisite relations among these definitions. Begin with [why random variables are needed](why-random-variables.qmd).

Read each family page as an **observation-process argument**, not as a catalog
entry. Ask what is random, what is fixed, why the support matches, which
independence or exchangeability assumptions are required, and which visible
feature would make the family inadequate.
